planting.note: Direct sow in fall in lean, alkaline or saline, gravelly soil in full sun; desert holly establishes best in the hottest, most mineral-poor sites and resents regular garden watering.

directions: Desert holly is a low, rounded saltbush of the hottest, most saline flats in the Mojave and Death Valley region, instantly recognizable for its stiff, holly-shaped, silvery-white leaves that reflect intense sun and give the plant its common name. Unlike most desert shrubs it stays most visually striking through the hottest part of summer, when its foliage turns its brightest silver, and takes on a duller gray-green cast during cooler, wetter months. Tiny inconspicuous flowers appear on separate male and female plants in spring, followed by small winged fruits on female shrubs. It thrives in alkaline, saline, gypsum-rich soils that few other plants tolerate and needs no irrigation once established, making it a distinctive foliage accent for a true low-desert xeriscape planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto loose, sandy desert wash soil in full sun; cheesebush germinates readily after winter rain and is best used to quickly stabilize disturbed wash-margin ground rather than as a long-term specimen shrub.

directions: Cheesebush is a fast-growing, short-lived pioneer shrub of sandy desert washes across the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, quickly colonizing disturbed or recently scoured wash bottoms where few other plants can establish. Its narrow, thread-like, pale green leaves and stems release a distinctive pungent odor likened to cheese when crushed or bruised, the source of both its common name and its old classification alongside the ragweeds. Inconspicuous greenish flowers in late summer and fall give way to small fruits surrounded by papery, straw-colored wings that cluster densely along the stems, creating a hazy, cottony look across whole wash bottoms at a distance. It needs no irrigation or soil amendment and is best treated as a quick-establishing erosion-control shrub, since individual plants typically decline and need replacement after five to ten years.

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into rocky, mineral desert soil in full sun; blackbrush germinates and establishes slowly and should be sited where it can remain undisturbed for decades, since mature stands rarely recover once destroyed by fire.

directions: Blackbrush is the defining, often near-monotypic shrub of the transition belt between Mojave Desert scrub and higher pinyon-juniper woodland, forming dense, even-aged stands across thousands of acres of rocky upper bajadas and mesas. Its rigid, intricately branched gray stems appear almost black when wet, and small pale yellow flowers lacking true petals (the color comes from petal-like sepals) open in spring directly on the bare, spine-tipped twigs before the sparse small leaves emerge. Growth is extremely slow and individual plants can persist for centuries, but because blackbrush does not resprout reliably after fire, established stands are highly vulnerable to disturbance from invasive annual grasses that raise fire frequency in its habitat. Plant in rocky, well-drained, mineral soil in full sun with no supplemental summer water, treating it as a long-term structural specimen rather than a fast-filling landscape shrub.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; turpentine broom is slow and often erratic to establish from seed and does best left undisturbed on a permanent rocky slope site once planted.

directions: Turpentine broom is a small, blue-green, nearly leafless shrublet of rocky slopes and washes across the Mojave and western Sonoran Deserts, its cylindrical stems dotted with oil glands that release a sharp citrus-and-turpentine scent when crushed, a trait it shares with its relatives in the citrus family. Small four-petaled, dark violet-purple flowers open along the stems in late winter and early spring, followed by distinctive two-lobed seed capsules that persist into summer. The gray-green to blue-green stems carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis in place of true leaves, an adaptation that reduces water loss in its hot, rocky habitat. Site it in full sun on lean, rocky, sharply drained soil and avoid rich amendments or regular watering, conditions the plant does not tolerate in cultivation.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant rooted cuttings into well-drained, rocky or sandy desert soil in full sun; Anderson's wolfberry leafs out quickly after winter rain and tolerates being cut back hard if it becomes too thorny and tangled.

directions: Anderson's wolfberry, also called desert thorn, is a dense, intricately branched, spiny shrub common along desert washes and rocky slopes throughout the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts, often among the first shrubs to leaf out and flower after winter rains. Small lavender-pink, tubular to bell-shaped flowers open from late winter into spring and are followed by bright red-orange berries that ripen through spring and summer, an important early-season food source for desert birds and small mammals. The narrow, fleshy gray-green leaves drop during extended drought, leaving the gray, thorny stem framework to carry the plant through dry periods before resprouting with rain. Plant in full sun in lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil and withhold summer irrigation once established, since the species is adapted to long dry spells punctuated by brief, intense rains.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; pale wolfberry tolerates somewhat cooler, higher desert sites than other Lycium species and needs no irrigation once its roots are established.

directions: Pale wolfberry, also known as rabbit thorn or pale desert-thorn, is a stiffly branched, spiny shrub found at slightly higher, cooler desert elevations than many of its Lycium relatives, ranging across the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau into rocky slopes and dry washes. Its pale gray-green, somewhat fleshy leaves set it apart from the darker-leaved Anderson's wolfberry, and its pale lavender to greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers open in spring before giving way to juicy orange-red berries traditionally gathered and eaten fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the region. The dense, spiny branch structure also provides valuable nesting and escape cover for desert birds and small wildlife. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil with no summer irrigation once roots are established, since wet soil during its dormant season is the chief cultivation hazard.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; Mojave aster blooms best with minimal supplemental water and benefits from an occasional hard cutback after flowering to keep the woody base from sprawling.

directions: Mojave aster is a woody-based perennial wildflower found on rocky slopes, washes, and desert pavement throughout the Mojave Desert, producing large lavender to white daisy-like flower heads with bright yellow centers from late winter through late spring, often lingering later into the season than most desert annuals. Its stiff, grayish, rough-textured leaves are slightly twisted along their length, the source of the species name tortifolia, and persist through the dry season on a low, rounded, semi-woody base. Established plants tolerate extreme heat and long drought on minimal supplemental water and serve as an important early-season nectar source for native desert bees and butterflies. Site it in full sun in lean, rocky, sharply drained soil and avoid rich garden conditions or regular watering, which shorten its naturally long bloom display and lifespan.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural winter stratification, or set out container plants in spring, into coarse, fast-draining rocky or sandy soil in full sun; avoid overwatering young plants, which rot quickly in moist soil.

directions: Nevada jointfir, also called Mojave Mormon tea, is a leafless, broom-like, gray-green shrub common on dry gravelly slopes and benches across the Mojave Desert and Great Basin, photosynthesizing through its slender, stiffly ascending, jointed stems rather than true leaves. Tiny, inconspicuous cone-like strobili appear at the stem joints in spring on separate male and female plants, and its grayer, more divergently branched habit distinguishes it in the field from the brighter green, more upright Ephedra viridis of higher pinyon-juniper country. Like other desert jointfirs, its dried stems have long been steeped by regional Indigenous peoples and later settlers into a mild, caffeine-free herbal tea, the source of the common name Mormon tea. It is essentially maintenance-free once established in lean, rocky, fast-draining soil and full sun, needing no supplemental water beyond its first year.

planting.note: Scarify seed and direct sow in fall into lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; Fremont's indigo bush needs no irrigation once established and declines quickly in rich or regularly watered garden soil.

directions: Fremont's indigo bush, also known as Fremont dalea, is a rounded, gray-haired shrub of dry rocky slopes and washes along the margins of the Mojave Desert and Great Basin, its finely divided, silvery-hairy foliage dotted with resin glands that give off a sharp, resinous scent when crushed. Small but showy purple to blue-violet pea-like flowers crowd along the stem tips in spring, drawing native bees, and are followed by small, resin-dotted seed pods. Like other desert daleas, it fixes nitrogen through root nodules, slowly improving the lean, rocky soils it grows in. Plant in full sun in sharply drained, mineral soil, scarifying seed before sowing to improve germination, and withhold summer irrigation once the shrub is established.
